meta.title: Prelude No. 1 in C major, BWV 846

provenance.author: Musicanyya practice material
provenance.basedOn: Johann Sebastian Bach, Prelude No. 1 in C major, BWV 846, from The Well-Tempered Clavier, Book I (compiled by 1722, public domain; Bach died 1750). 35 measures, consisting almost entirely of a one-bar broken-chord figure (an eighth rest plus six 16th notes, played twice per bar) over a sustained bass note and a tied inner voice, with a written-out flourish replacing the repeat in the final three bars.

meta.subtitle: from The Well-Tempered Clavier, Book I
meta.trains: Continuous right-hand arpeggiation over a sustained left-hand bass and an inner tied suspension voice; harmonic listening bar-to-bar (each measure is one implied chord); evenness of tone as the hand shifts position across 35 measures without a rest longer than an eighth note.

meta.subtitle: Arabeske
meta.trains: Quick 16th-note turn figures answered by a light eighth-note tag, alternating with a lyrical dotted-quarter melody, over a steady broken-chord left hand in A minor - finger agility and voicing a short melodic cell cleanly at a scherzando tempo.

meta.title: Prelude in C minor, Op. 28 No. 20
meta.subtitle: "Funeral March"
meta.trains: Dense, widely-spread four- and five-note block chords in both hands (up to a minor 10th), a full ff-to-pp dynamic range with two written crescendi, and a two-layer right-hand texture (a sustained chord against a decorative turn figure) that asks for careful voicing and pedalling rather than finger speed.
limitations: Written pedal is not played by the engine (facts.hasPedal is informational only).

Slurs and the exact hairpin start/stop beat positions from the source engraving are approximated, not reproduced to the exact beat; they do not change the sounding pitches, rhythm or overall dynamic shape.

meta.subtitle: Spiritoso
meta.trains: A brisk single-line melody in the right hand (scale runs, octave leaps, broken octaves) over a light left hand of mostly quarter, half and whole notes, with broken-chord eighths in bars 9, 11, 32 and 34: an exposition that moves to G major, a short development that turns to C minor (bars 16-23), and the return in C - reading fluency and a fast, even tempo more than technical difficulty.

meta.title: Für Elise, WoO 59

provenance.credit: Typeset by Stelios Samelis for the Mutopia Project (Mutopia-2015/08/18-931) from the Breitkopf & Härtel edition of 1888, and placed in the public domain by the typesetter.
provenance.note: Converted from Mutopia's LilyPond source to MusicXML (notes, rests, repeats and voltas, grace notes, triplets, 8va, clefs, slurs, dynamics, pedal); beams and accidentals then completed by pnpm library:engrave. Checked mechanically: all 902 non-grace notes match Mutopia's own MIDI file in pitch and written onset, and the three grace notes are the only notes the MIDI has in addition. 106 measures, as in Mutopia's engraving.

meta.subtitle: Complete piece, from the Breitkopf & Härtel edition (1888) via the Mutopia Project
meta.trains: The whole rondo as Beethoven wrote it: the A theme over broken-chord bass, the F-major episode with its grace notes and 32nd-note figures, the agitated C section over a repeated bass pedal, and the triplet arpeggio run up under an 8va and back down chromatically.
limitations: The first-ending bar and the final bar are two eighths long (together with the pickup they make a full bar, as printed), so opening the piece shows an information notice about measure length.

meta.title: Morning Mood

provenance.credit: G. Schirmer, New York, 1899: First and Second Orchestra Suites from the Music to Peer Gynt, arranged for pianoforte by the composer; Morgenstimmung edited and fingered by Louis Oesterle (Internet Archive 31761045200615).
provenance.note: There is no public-domain machine-readable copy, so the piano part was transcribed twice from the 1899 print, bar by bar, by two separate sessions that never saw each other's work (transcriptions A and B, our own readings, CC0). This item is converted from transcription A with pnpm library:convert-ly and completed by pnpm library:engrave; its audit record compares it note by note with transcription B, every difference settled against the print, and with the print page by page. Two changes from the print: in bars 77-78 the right hand's chords, which the print writes on the lower staff, are printed on the upper staff, so the level check (which measures chord spans per printed staff) does not count them with the left hand; and in bars 64-65 the E4 that the melody shares with the lower voice (one head with two stems) is written once, in the lower voice, so it is one key to play. The Orchestra - flute, oboe, strings with a separate cello line, and horns - is our own orchestration in the style of Grieg's (CC0), generated from the piano part: every Orchestra note doubles a piano note, so nothing in it is new music, and it is not Grieg's orchestral score.

meta.subtitle: Peer Gynt Suite No. 1, Op. 46 No. 1 - the composer's piano arrangement, with orchestra
meta.trains: Grieg's own piano version of the sunrise from Peer Gynt: a pastoral 6/8 melody passed between the hands over held chords and wide left-hand tenths, the forte climax in full chords, the left-hand melody under right-hand figuration, trills with their endings, and the quiet return over a pedal note.

meta.title: Gymnopedie No. 1

meta.subtitle: Complete piece, from the Dover edition via the Mutopia Project
meta.trains: A wide-spanning left hand alternating a low bass note with a chord high above it (up to a two-and-a-half-octave leap), unmarked, player-chosen pedalling, ties held across barlines and soft, patient dynamic shading (pp/p/f) at a slow tempo.

meta.subtitle: Hymn tune "New Britain", simple two-hand setting in 3/4
meta.trains: A well-known pentatonic melody with a one-beat pickup, in half, quarter and a few eighth notes, over a single sustained bass note per bar - gentle two-hand reading at a slow tempo.

meta.title: Fur Elise (opening motif, arranged for absolute beginners)

provenance.author: Musicanyya practice material
provenance.basedOn: Beethoven, Fur Elise, WoO 59 (public domain, composed c. 1810), opening only. The quoted bars were checked against the Mutopia Project's public-domain LilyPond engraving (piece-info id 931, fur_Elise_WoO59.ly, typeset by Stelios Samelis from the Breitkopf & Härtel edition of 1888); the audit record content/library/audit/repertoire/beginner/fur-elise-theme-16-bar.json re-runs that check.
provenance.note: A different, much simpler arrangement from the intermediate Fur Elise item. The pickup and bars 1-8 follow Beethoven's melody with every value doubled (3/8 written as 3/4), with the changes listed in departures; bars 9-16 repeat bars 5-8. The left hand is a single sustained bass note per bar and rests under the opening figure, as in Beethoven's own texture there. 17 written measures (a one-beat pickup plus 16 bars) at quarter = 60.

meta.subtitle: 16-bar beginner arrangement: melody with a single bass note per bar
meta.trains: The famous opening motif read at a gentle tempo with eighth notes at most, over a single left-hand bass note per bar - the hands barely need to coordinate.
departures: Metre and values: Beethoven's 3/8 is written as 3/4 with every note value doubled (sixteenths become eighths).
Bar 1: E, D-sharp (eighths), E (quarter), B, D (eighths); Beethoven has six even notes E-D#-E-B-D-C, so the C before bar 2's A is left out and no more than four equal notes follow each other.
Bars 3-4: no accidentals after bar 1 - G instead of G-sharp in bar 3, D instead of D-sharp at the end of bar 4.
Bars 5-8 are our own shortened version of Beethoven's bars 5-8: bar 5 is E, D, C, B (Beethoven: E, D-sharp, E, B, D, C), bar 7 repeats bar 3 (Beethoven: B, E, C, B), and bar 8 ends on A.
Bars 9-12 and 13-16 repeat bars 5-8.
Left hand: our own single bass note per bar (A or E) instead of Beethoven's broken chords.

meta.title: Greensleeves (arranged for beginners)

provenance.author: Musicanyya practice material
provenance.basedOn: Traditional English melody "Greensleeves" (public domain), in the form of the hymn tune "Greensleeves" as typeset by the Mutopia Project (piece-info id 1247, greensleeves.ly, by Steve Dunlop from www.cyberhymnal.org, public domain). The melody is the Soprano of that file; the audit record content/library/audit/repertoire/beginner/greensleeves.json re-checks it note by note.
provenance.note: An eighth-note pickup and 16 bars in E minor at quarter = 76. The right hand follows the source's melody note for note, with the changes listed in departures; the left hand holds one bass note per bar.

meta.subtitle: Traditional English melody, simple two-hand setting in 3/4
meta.trains: A well-known minor-key melody in quarters and eighths over a single sustained bass note per bar - reading two staves together at a gentle tempo.
departures: Metre and rhythm: the tune's 6/8 is written as 3/4 (the same bar length), and every dotted-eighth-and-sixteenth pair is played as two even eighths.
No raised 6th or 7th: D instead of D-sharp (bars 3, 7, 11, 12, 15), C instead of C-sharp (bar 9), so the piece stays within the Beginner limit on accidentals.
Bars 7 and 15: the neighbour-note figure D#-C#-D# is played as one D, and the bar is G (quarter), F-sharp and E (eighths), D (quarter), so no more than four equal notes follow each other.
Bar 12: the last note is B4, an octave above the source's B3, so the jump to bar 13 stays within an octave.
Left hand: our own single held bass note per bar, taken from the source's bass line (G in bars 9 and 13, where its bass moves to G under the melody's C), instead of its four-part harmony.

meta.title: Jingle Bells (opening refrain, arranged for beginners)

provenance.author: Musicanyya practice material
provenance.basedOn: James Lord Pierpont's song, copyrighted September 16, 1857 as "The One Horse Open Sleigh" and reissued in 1859 as "Jingle Bells" (public domain). The chorus here is the modern one, checked against "Jingle, Bells" arr. George Rosey (copyright 1908) in The most popular home songs (New York, 1913), pp. 54-55. Pierpont's 1857 chorus has a different tune.
provenance.note: Only the familiar refrain ("Jingle bells, jingle bells, jingle all the way / Oh what fun it is to ride in a one-horse open sleigh") is arranged here, 8 bars, key of C major, quarter=96 - not the full song with its verses. The changes are listed in departures. The left-hand bass note per bar is our own.

meta.subtitle: "Jingle bells, jingle bells, jingle all the way" - simple two-hand setting
meta.trains: A very well-known, mostly repeated-note and stepwise melody in quarter/half notes over a single sustained bass note per bar, at a brisk tempo.
departures: Only the chorus, once, with its final ending ("...one-horse open sleigh!"); the verses are left out.
Key and values: C major (the 1908 printing is in G), with every note value doubled (eighths become quarters).
Bars 3 and 5: the dotted figure on "all the" and the dotted-and-sixteenth notes of "Oh! what fun it is" are even quarters; bars 4 and 8: the last note is held for the whole bar.
Bars 5-6: "in a" is sung on one note E (the printing has two sixteenths).
Left hand: our own single bass note per bar; the printing has its own piano part.

meta.title: Mary Had a Little Lamb (arranged for beginners)

provenance.author: Musicanyya practice material
provenance.basedOn: Sarah Josepha Hale's poem "Mary's Lamb" (Boston, 1830). The tune is the traditional one also sung as "Merrily We Roll Along"; it was checked against The child's own music book (ed. A. E. Wier, New York, 1918), p. 49, where it is printed in F major. Both are public domain.
provenance.note: 8-bar beginner form in F major (the key of the 1918 printing), so the melody sits in a single five-finger hand position (F-G-A-Bb-C), quarter=96. The left-hand single bass note per bar (I-V) is our own simple setting.

meta.subtitle: Traditional American melody, five-finger setting in F major
meta.trains: A very well-known three/four-note melody that never leaves a five-finger hand position, over a single sustained bass note per bar - an easy first piece for a fixed hand position.
departures: Values doubled: each bar is one 2/4 bar of the familiar tune written in 4/4 (eighths become quarters).
Rhythm made plain: the dotted "Ma-ry" in bars 1 and 5 is two even notes, and the last F in bar 8 is held for the whole bar.
Left hand: our own single bass note per bar; the printing has its own piano part.

meta.title: Ode to Joy (theme, arranged for beginners)

provenance.author: Musicanyya practice material
provenance.basedOn: Beethoven, "Ode to Joy" theme (Symphony No. 9, 4th movement; public domain). The melody was checked note by note against the Soprano of the Mutopia Project's public-domain hymn setting (piece-info id 528, ode.ly, typeset by Peter Chubb), transposed from G to C major; the audit record content/library/audit/repertoire/beginner/ode-to-joy.json re-runs that check. Rhythm checked by eye against the first edition (Schott, 1826).
provenance.note: The first two 4-bar phrases only, ending on the tonic; not the complete theme. Bars 4 and 8 keep Beethoven's dotted figure (dotted quarter, eighth, half).

meta.subtitle: Theme from Symphony No. 9, simple two-hand arrangement
meta.trains: A simple stepwise melody with steady quarter notes over static left-hand chords - an easy introduction to playing both hands together.
departures: Bars 1-8 only (the first two phrases); the theme's middle phrase and return (its bars 9-16) are left out.
Key: C major (Beethoven's theme is in D major; the hymn setting it was checked against is in G major).
Left hand: our own block chords, one per bar (C, G, F in bar 7) and two in bar 8 (G, then C).

meta.title: Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star (arranged for beginners)

provenance.author: Musicanyya practice material
provenance.basedOn: The tune "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star" is the French melody "Ah! vous dirai-je, Maman", first printed c. 1761 (public domain); the English text is Jane Taylor's 1806 poem, also public domain. The melody was checked against The child's own music book (ed. A. E. Wier, New York, 1918), p. 116, and compared with the theme of Mozart's variations K. 265 (Paris: Porro, c. 1801).
provenance.note: A-B-A form in 12 bars of 4/4 (three 4-bar phrases; the last repeats the first), key of C major, quarter=92. The melody was checked against a 1918 printing of the song (see the audit record). The left-hand bass note per bar is our own simple setting.

meta.subtitle: Traditional French melody, simple two-hand setting in 4/4
meta.trains: A very well-known stepwise-and-small-leap melody in quarter and half notes, over a single sustained bass note per bar - an easy first tune for reading two staves together.
departures: Key: C major (the 1918 printing it was checked against is in F).
Metre: two 2/4 bars of the 1918 printing make one 4/4 bar (note values unchanged).
The plain nursery form: Mozart's K. 265 theme has D, D-E, C in bars 4 and 12, E, E, D, D in bar 6 and a trilled E-F in bar 8.
Left hand: our own single bass note per bar; the printing has its own piano part.

meta.title: Innocence (25 Etudes faciles, Op. 100, No. 5 - opening strain, arranged)

provenance.author: Musicanyya practice material
provenance.basedOn: Burgmuller, 25 Etudes faciles et progressives, Op. 100, No. 5 "Innocence" (public domain, published 1852). Measures 1-11 (both hands, right-hand 16th-note and 8th-note pitches and rhythm, left-hand dotted-half triads) were checked note-by-note against the Mutopia Project's public-domain LilyPond edition (piece-info id 214, 25EF-05, typeset by Bas Wassink, key F major, Moderato).
provenance.note: This is our own re-engraving, not a copy of the Mutopia file, and it is an arrangement of the opening strain only (11 of the source's measures): the source's own second strain closes with a more virtuosic ottava-displaced descending/ascending run and a forte chord that we judged too advanced for this shelf slot, so measures 12-16 here are our own closing - a restatement of the opening's 16th-note turn figure (same as measures 1, matching the source's own written repeat structure) followed by a simple three-chord plagal-flavoured cadence, built from the piece's own motifs rather than transcribed from the source's actual ending.

meta.subtitle: Unschuld - opening strain, our own closing
meta.trains: A graceful right-hand melody mixing 16th-note turns with dotted-quarter/eighth figures over a sustained left-hand triad in each bar, in 3/4 at a moderate tempo - light articulation and phrase shading more than raw technique.
departures: Bars 12-16 are our own close.

meta.title: Für Elise (theme, arranged for this app)

provenance.author: Musicanyya practice material
provenance.basedOn: Beethoven, Für Elise, WoO 59 (public domain, composed c. 1810). A-section pitches and rhythm were checked against the Mutopia Project's public-domain LilyPond engraving (piece-info id 931, fur_Elise_WoO59.ly, typeset by Stelios Samelis) before this transcription.
provenance.note: Theme only: the pickup and bars 1-8 of WoO 59, through the theme's first cadence on the A-minor tonic. The B and C sections of the complete piece are not included, and the ending is simplified to a single-pass cadence instead of the repeat back to bar 1.

meta.subtitle: Pickup and bars 1-8 of WoO 59, with a single-pass ending
meta.trains: Melodic phrasing over a broken-chord left-hand accompaniment, with a chromatic neighbour-note motif.
departures: Theme only: the pickup and bars 1-8 of WoO 59; the rest of the piece is left out.
Bar 8 ends the piece: the final A is held as a dotted quarter to fill the bar, instead of the first ending's quarter note and the repeat back to the start.

meta.title: Musette in D major, BWV Anh. 126

provenance.credit: Typeset by Allen Garvin for the Mutopia Project (Mutopia-2013/01/06-79) from the Bach-Gesellschaft edition, and placed in the public domain by the typesetter.
provenance.note: Converted from Mutopia's LilyPond source to MusicXML by pnpm library:convert-ly (notes, rests, repeats and voltas, grace notes, clefs, slurs, dynamics); beams and accidentals then completed by pnpm library:engrave. Checked mechanically against the LilyPond source and Mutopia's own MIDI file (audit record). The Notebook copy is unsigned and its composer is unknown; it is listed in the appendix (Anhang) of doubtful works in the Bach-Werke-Verzeichnis.

meta.subtitle: from the Notebook for Anna Magdalena Bach (1725)
meta.trains: A bagpipe dance in 2/4 over a drone: the left hand leaps in octaves (on D, then A and E) and doubles the right hand in bars 3–4 and 7–8; the right hand has sixteenth-note runs and eighth-note figures. The second half moves to A major over a long E pedal (G sharp, D sharp, D natural) and ends there; the fermata in bar 8 marks where a da capo would end (the edition prints no da capo, so none is played). Both halves repeated.

meta.title: Minuet in G major, BWV Anh. 114

provenance.credit: Typeset by Allen Garvin for the Mutopia Project (Mutopia-2017/01/19-75) from the Bach-Gesellschaft edition, and placed in the public domain by the typesetter.
provenance.note: Converted from Mutopia's LilyPond source to MusicXML by pnpm library:convert-ly (notes, rests, repeats and voltas, grace notes, clefs, slurs, dynamics); beams and accidentals then completed by pnpm library:engrave. Checked mechanically against the LilyPond source and Mutopia's own MIDI file (audit record). Long known as "Bach's Minuet in G"; the Notebook copy is unsigned and it is now attributed to Christian Petzold (1677-1733), as the source itself notes.

meta.subtitle: from the Notebook for Anna Magdalena Bach (1725)
meta.trains: Two independent lines in 3/4: a right-hand melody of stepwise eighth-note runs and leaps against a left hand that moves in its own line of mostly dotted-half, half and quarter notes; mordents (bars 3, 5, 11, 13), a grace note in bar 8 and a short trill in bar 30, and a second half that turns to D major (C sharp) before coming home. Both halves repeated.

provenance.credit: Typeset by Allen Garvin for the Mutopia Project (Mutopia-2015/08/21-76) from the Bach-Gesellschaft edition, and placed in the public domain by the typesetter.
provenance.note: Converted from Mutopia's LilyPond source to MusicXML by pnpm library:convert-ly (notes, rests, repeats and voltas, grace notes, clefs, slurs, dynamics); beams and accidentals then completed by pnpm library:engrave. Checked mechanically against the LilyPond source and Mutopia's own MIDI file (audit record). The Notebook copy is unsigned; it is attributed to Christian Petzold (1677-1733), as the source itself notes.

meta.subtitle: from the Notebook for Anna Magdalena Bach (1725)
meta.trains: The G major minuet’s companion in the minor: the same two-line minuet texture in 3/4, reading B flat and E flat from the key, F sharp as the leading note, and E natural and B natural as the music passes through B flat major and F major before returning home; mordents (bars 13, 22) and short trills (bars 8, 9, 15, 31). Both halves repeated.
